title: What feminism got right, and where Islam differs
thesis: Islam agrees with the core early feminist demands (property, education, consent, protection from abuse) and established most of them in the seventh century. It parts company with parts of later feminism on identical roles, sexual autonomy and the status of the family. A debater should concede the agreement before stating the differences.
premises: “Feminism” covers incompatible positions (liberal, difference, radical, and Muslim feminists), so the first question to ask is which claim is being made.
The founding demands were property rights, education, consent to marriage and protection from violence, and Islam’s sources establish each of these.

Later claims, such as that gender is wholly a social construct, that sexual freedom is liberation and that family roles are oppression, conflict with Islamic teaching, and a Muslim can say so while affirming women’s rights.
conclusion: A Muslim can affirm women’s dignity and rights fully without adopting every feminist doctrine as a package, and should be honest where Muslim societies have fallen short of their own sources.
evidence: Property. “For men is a share of what the parents and relatives leave, and for women is a share” (4:7). “For women is a share of what they have earned” (4:32). The dowry belongs to the bride: “Give women their dowries as a gift” (4:4). In England, a married woman’s property passed to her husband until the Married Women’s Property Acts of 1870 and 1882.

Education. Women came to the Prophet ﷺ and said men had taken all his time, so he set aside a day for them and taught them (Bukhari 101). Aisha became one of the great teachers of the first generation.
The vote, for context. Women got the vote in the United States in 1920, in Britain on equal terms in 1928, in France in 1944 and in Swiss federal elections in 1971.

Where Muslim societies fail. Denying daughters their inheritance, their education or a say in marriage contradicts the sources. When the Taliban banned girls’ secondary schooling (2021) and women’s university education (2022), Al-Azhar and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation criticised the decisions as contrary to Islam.
Where Islam differs: sameness. The Quran states “the male is not like the female” (3:36) and treats sex as real and meaningful (see the section on sexuality and gender).
Where Islam differs: motherhood. A man asked who most deserved his good company and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Your mother”, three times, “then your father” (Bukhari 5971, Muslim 2548).
Where Islam differs: sexual ethics. Sex is lawful only within marriage for both sexes, which is a different understanding of liberation from the one in most Western feminism.

objections.q: “Muslim feminists like Amina Wadud show Islam can be feminist.”
objections.a: Some Muslim women scholars have raised real issues about patriarchal readings, and challenging culture presented as religion is legitimate. But when a reading sets aside explicit rulings (Wadud led a mixed-gender Friday prayer in New York in 2005), the great majority of scholars reject it. Distinguish between correcting a cultural reading and discarding a text.

Some are, and often in ways the sources forbid: denying inheritance, schooling or consent. Others are not, and several Muslim-majority countries have elected women as heads of government (Benazir Bhutto in Pakistan in 1988, Tansu Çiller in Turkey, Khaleda Zia and Sheikh Hasina in Bangladesh, Megawati Sukarnoputri in Indonesia). The question is whether the rule is in the sources, not whether every society follows it.

practice.q: You cannot call yourself pro-woman unless you accept feminism.
practice.a: Feminism is several different positions, so tell me which one. If you mean property, education, consent and protection from violence, Islam established those in the seventh century (4:7, 4:32, Bukhari 101) when most legal systems did not, and I criticise Muslim societies that deny them. If you mean that sex roles are only a social construct or that sexual freedom is liberation, I disagree and I will say why. Rejecting a package is not the same as rejecting women’s dignity.

summary: Islam gave women property, education and consent early, and Muslims should condemn societies that deny them; it differs from parts of later feminism on identical roles, sexual autonomy and the family.

title: Women in public life: scholars, traders, advisers and rulers
thesis: Islamic history shows women as traders, scholars, teachers, advisers, fighters and, rarely, rulers. The main objection, Bukhari 4425, is read by most jurists as restricting the supreme leadership of the community, and other public roles remain open.
premises: A claim that Islam confines women to the home must be tested against the record of the first generations and later centuries.
The record shows women in commerce, scholarship, counsel and defence, with the Prophet’s ﷺ approval.
The one text that limits a public role speaks about a specific appointment, and scholars differ on how far it extends.
conclusion: Islam does not keep women out of public life. It limits at most the highest office of the community in the majority view, and Muslim history is full of women exercising authority in knowledge, trade and politics.
evidence: Khadija. A successful merchant who hired Muhammad ﷺ to trade for her before their marriage (Ibn Ishaq), and the first person to believe in him.
Umm Salama at Hudaybiyyah. When the Companions hesitated to obey the order to slaughter and shave after the treaty, the Prophet ﷺ followed Umm Salama’s advice, and they obeyed (Bukhari 2731-2732).
Aisha. She narrated over two thousand hadith and corrected senior Companions, which al-Zarkashi collected in al-Ijaba li-irad ma istadrakat-hu ‘A’isha ‘ala al-sahaba.

Women scholars. Mohammad Akram Nadwi’s al-Muhaddithat documents thousands of women hadith scholars across the centuries. Karima al-Marwaziyya (d. 1070) was one of the most sought-after transmitters of Sahih al-Bukhari.
Defenders. Nusayba bint Ka‘b defended the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa‘d).
Rulers. Arwa al-Sulayhi ruled Yemen (d. 1138), Shajar al-Durr was sultana of Egypt in 1250, Razia Sultan ruled Delhi in 1236-40, and several sultanas ruled Aceh in the seventeenth century.

The hadith. “A people who entrust their affairs to a woman will not prosper” (Bukhari 4425) was said when the Prophet ﷺ learned the Persians had crowned the daughter of Khosrow. The majority hold it restricts the supreme leadership (al-imama al-kubra) to men. Abu Hanifa allowed women as judges in matters where their testimony is accepted, and al-Tabari is reported to have allowed it in all matters.

objections.q: “So a woman cannot be head of state in Islam.”
objections.a: Most classical jurists held that the supreme leadership of the community is for a man, and a few contemporary scholars argue the hadith concerns a specific absolute monarchy. State the majority view and say the disagreement exists. In the modern state, where the head of government is not the caliph, many Muslim scholars and countries accept women in the highest offices.

objections.q: “Women are told to stay at home (33:33).”
objections.a: 33:33 is addressed to the Prophet’s ﷺ wives, who held a special status (33:32), and the same wives travelled, taught and advised. Women in general prayed in the mosque, traded and taught in the Prophet’s time. The ruling concerns decorum, not exclusion.

practice.q: Islam locks women in the home.
practice.a: Look at the record: Khadija was a merchant who employed the Prophet ﷺ, Umm Salama’s advice resolved the crisis at Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari 2731), Aisha taught and corrected Companions, thousands of women were hadith scholars, and queens ruled in Yemen, Egypt and Delhi. There is a majority opinion that the top office of the whole community is for men, based on Bukhari 4425, and I would state that openly. Everything else, from scholarship to commerce, was open.

summary: Women were merchants, scholars, advisers, defenders and rulers in Muslim history. The one restriction, from Bukhari 4425, is read by most as limiting the supreme leadership of the community.

title: Marriage: consent, the dowry and a wife’s way out
thesis: In Islamic law a marriage needs the bride’s consent, the dowry is her own property, and she can leave through khul‘ or judicial dissolution. Forced marriage violates the law, and the Prophet ﷺ annulled one.
premises: A marriage contract is valid only with the free consent of both parties.
The wife receives a dowry that is hers alone and can stipulate conditions in the contract.
She has legal routes out of a marriage she cannot continue.
conclusion: Islamic marriage law gives the woman consent, property and an exit, and a marriage forced on her is not valid in Islam.
evidence: Consent. “A previously married woman is not to be married until she is consulted, and a virgin is not to be married until her permission is sought.” They asked how a virgin gives permission and he said: “By her silence” (Bukhari 5136).

A forced marriage annulled. Khansa bint Khidham’s father married her against her will, and the Prophet ﷺ annulled the marriage (Bukhari 5138). In another report a girl said her father had married her to his nephew; the Prophet ﷺ gave her the choice, and she replied that she accepted but wanted women to know that fathers have no power to force them (Ibn Majah 1874).
The dowry. “Give women their dowries as a gift” (4:4). It is the wife’s property and she may spend it as she wishes.

Conditions. “The conditions most deserving to be fulfilled are those by which you make intimacy lawful” (Bukhari 2721), which the Hanbali school applies to conditions such as no second wife or no relocation.

Khul‘. Habiba bint Sahl told the Prophet ﷺ she did not fault her husband Thabit ibn Qays’s character or religion but could not live with him; he asked her to return the garden she had received from him and told Thabit to accept it and divorce her (Bukhari 5273). See also 2:229.

Barira. A freed slave woman chose to leave her husband Mughith. The Prophet ﷺ interceded for him, she asked whether he was commanding her, he said he was only interceding, and she declined (Bukhari 5283).
Court-ordered divorce. The jurists, especially the Malikis, allow a judge to dissolve a marriage for harm, non-maintenance or desertion.

objections.q: “The wali requirement means a woman cannot choose her own husband.”
objections.a: The majority require a guardian for the marriage as protection and public witness, and that guardian cannot force her against her consent (Bukhari 5136, 5138). The Hanafi school holds that an adult woman may contract her own marriage. The shared principle is that her consent is required.

objections.q: “Men can divorce by talaq but women cannot.”
objections.a: The procedures differ: the husband pronounces talaq, and the wife can obtain khul‘ or a judicial dissolution, and can be given the power to divorce herself (tafwid) in the contract. Defend the substance, that she has routes out, and say that in practice courts and customs vary, which is often where abuses occur.

practice.q: Muslim women are married off against their will.
practice.a: That is forced marriage and Islamic law does not accept it. The Prophet ﷺ said a woman must be asked and her permission sought (Bukhari 5136), and when Khansa’s father married her against her will, he annulled it (Bukhari 5138). She also owns her dowry (4:4) and can leave through khul‘ (Bukhari 5273). Where forced marriages happen, they come from custom and they violate the sources.

summary: A valid Islamic marriage requires the bride’s consent (Bukhari 5136), the Prophet ﷺ annulled a forced one (5138), the dowry is hers, and she can leave through khul‘ (5273) or the court.

title: Honour killing, forced marriage and FGM: customs, not Islamic law
thesis: Honour killing and forced marriage are forbidden by Islamic law. FGM is not in the Quran, its hadith basis is weak and major Muslim institutions now prohibit it, though some classical jurists recommended or required it. State the record honestly, because the strongest reply concedes what is true.
premises: A practice is Islamic only if the sources and recognised jurists support it, and its prevalence among Muslims does not show that.
Killing outside a court is murder in Islamic law, and a charge of unchastity needs four eyewitnesses or a confession.
On FGM, the Quran is silent, the hadith evidence is weak and classical opinion was divided, and modern Muslim authorities have prohibited it on the ground of harm.
conclusion: Honour killings and forced marriage are crimes under Islamic law, and FGM is a disputed custom that Islamic principles of preventing harm now lead major authorities to prohibit.
evidence: Killing. “Whoever kills a soul unjustly… it is as if he had killed all mankind” (5:32); “Do not kill the soul that Allah has made sacred except by right” (17:33). A father or brother has no right to execute anyone.

The standard of proof. Zina requires four eyewitnesses to the act itself (24:13), and a false accusation without them is punished with eighty lashes (24:4). In li‘an a husband who accuses his wife without witnesses must swear oaths, not kill (24:6-9).

Not Islamic alone. Honour-based killings are reported among Hindus, Sikhs and Christians too, for example in parts of India, and Italy’s penal code gave reduced sentences for “crimes of honour” until 1981, so they cannot be traced to Islam alone.
Forced marriage. Invalid, as in the previous argument (Bukhari 5136, 5138).

FGM: the sources. The Quran does not mention it. The report usually cited (Abu Dawud 5271) advises “do not cut severely”, and Abu Dawud himself said that it is weak. The classical schools differ: some Shafi‘i texts call it obligatory, while the Hanafis, Malikis and Hanbalis describe it as a recommended or “honourable” custom for women.
FGM: the practice. UNICEF notes that FGM is found among Muslims, Christians and followers of traditional religions in the places where it occurs.

Modern rulings. In 2007, after a girl’s death, Egypt’s Grand Mufti Ali Gomaa and Al-Azhar scholars declared the practice forbidden, on the principle “no harm and no reciprocating harm” (Ibn Majah 2341).

objections.q: “Muslims do it, so it is Islamic.”
objections.a: Prevalence shows custom, not doctrine. Honour killings and FGM also occur among non-Muslims, and many Muslim societies do not practise them. The test is what the sources and the scholars say, and on honour killing the sources are clear, while on FGM the better-supported modern position forbids it.

That is true, and a Muslim should say so. Those opinions were based on a weak report and on the medical knowledge of their time. The jurists’ own principle that harm must be removed is why contemporary bodies, among them Al-Azhar’s scholars and Egypt’s Dar al-Ifta, prohibit it.

practice.q: Honour killings and genital cutting show what Islam does to women.
practice.a: On honour killing, Islamic law calls killing outside a court murder (5:32, 17:33) and demands four eyewitnesses before an accusation of zina (24:4, 24:13), so nothing in the law permits it, and it occurs in other religions too. On FGM, it is not in the Quran, the hadith cited is weak by its own collector’s verdict, some classical jurists did recommend it, and today Egypt’s Grand Mufti and Al-Azhar’s scholars forbid it. I condemn both, and I am telling you what the sources say and where scholars differed.

summary: Honour killing and forced marriage are forbidden by Islamic law. FGM has no Quranic basis, a weak hadith, mixed classical opinion and is now prohibited by major authorities; state the history honestly.
